name: mediator
intent: Define an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact, so that colleagues reference only that hub instead of each other and the coordination logic can vary independently of the objects it coordinates.
problem: Objects in a group call each other's methods directly, so each one must know and depend on many others. Every additional participant or interaction rule multiplies the references, the classes become hard to change or reuse in another composition, and a change to one collaboration ripples through every object that holds pointers to its peers.
context: In-process collaboration among a bounded, known set of objects - dialog widgets, entity or service clusters, editor/build-tool components, game entities - where the interaction rules are not stable and the participants must stay reusable outside this specific assembly. It applies when direct references would create a many-to-many web, the collaborators can agree on one narrow notification protocol, and the coordination can be centralised without crossing a process or network boundary.
benefits: Colleagues depend on one mediator interface instead of on N-1 peers: the many-to-many web becomes a star with O(N) references instead of O(N^2).
The interaction rules live in one place, so changing how participants cooperate is one edit in the hub rather than a hunt through every caller.
Colleagues become reusable in other compositions because they no longer know their peers; a different mediator rewires the same participants.
The protocol is small and explicit (usually a single notify/emit entry point), which makes the collaboration testable against a stub mediator and fake colleagues.
New colleagues and new mediation strategies plug in without touching the participants, and control flow can be observed, logged or intercepted in one place.
Typed event vocabularies (sealed interfaces, discriminated unions, record types) enable compiler-verified exhaustiveness checking, catching missing handler cases at compile time rather than runtime.
tradeoffs: The mediator can degenerate into a god object: coordination rules accumulate until the hub holds all the logic and colleagues become data holders - the pattern's best-known failure mode.
Indirection costs: every interaction gains a hop, an event vocabulary and a dispatch to maintain, and behaviour can no longer be read off a single colleague, so debugging follows the hub.
Centralisation creates a convergence point: one hub serialises routing and is the natural home of contention, back-pressure, or a single blocking/throw-raising handler that stalls every participant.
The coupling relocates rather than disappears: colleagues still depend on the mediator interface and the mediator depends on every colleague type, so protocol changes touch the hub and all senders.
Listener lifetime becomes a leak hazard: a hub that holds colleagues strongly keeps them alive, so weak references, explicit unregistration or deterministic teardown must be part of the design.
In typed languages, growing the sealed event hierarchy requires recompiling all participants that reference it; in dynamic languages the flexibility may hide runtime typos.

participants.responsibility: Declares the coordination interface colleagues use to talk to the hub - typically one notify(sender, event) entry point - and exposes nothing about individual colleagues' internals.
Implements the interaction rules, knows (and sometimes owns the lifetime of) the concrete colleagues, and decides what each notification triggers.
Base role of the participants: holds a reference to the abstract mediator and routes every outgoing interaction through it instead of calling peers directly.
A concrete participant (button, form field, entity, service) that keeps its own domain behaviour and only announces events or requests to the mediator.

use_cases: Dialog and form assemblies in which widgets enable, validate, prefill or hide each other - the canonical authentication-dialog example.
Wizards, checkout and onboarding flows whose steps must stay individually reusable across different flows.
In-process plugin or handler clusters (editor, IDE, build tool) where components announce events and one hub decides which others react.
Game scenes and simulation UIs where entities communicate through a coordinator instead of holding references to one another.
Chat rooms, collaboration sessions and presence hubs: a room object routes messages between participants that never address each other directly.
Unit tests: a stub mediator lets each colleague be exercised without constructing the whole collaboration.

Microservices orchestration layer: a process mediator (not an in-process object) coordinates distributed transactions, saga steps or chained API calls where services must not call each other directly.

CQRS command/query separation: MediatR-style request handlers route commands to write models and queries to read models, centralising the routing decision and enabling independent optimisation of read and write paths.

Workflow engines and saga coordinators: a mediator or process manager holds process state, decides next steps from incoming events and drives long-running business transactions across bounded contexts.

Event-driven UI coordination in modern frameworks: React context, Angular services or Vuex/Pinia stores act as in-process mediators that coordinate cross-component state without components holding direct cross-references.

Air traffic control and simulation systems: a central coordinator (control tower) mediates all communications so that aircraft never address each other directly — the canonical real-world analogy for the pattern.
Dashboard analytics platforms: filter panels, charts, tables and maps that must react to shared data selections without coupling to each other's internal representations.
Micro-frontend coordination: shared event buses enable separate frontend applications to communicate without direct cross-app dependencies.
IoT device orchestration: a central hub coordinates device state and triggers actions across heterogeneous hardware without devices calling each other directly.

MediatR (.NET): the official in-process mediator routes typed requests, commands, queries, notifications and events to handlers, providing a concrete request/handler implementation of this pattern without a transport.

MassTransit Mediator (.NET): its transport-free in-process mediator dispatches Send/Publish messages to consumers, handlers and sagas, with request/response, runtime connect/disconnect and middleware for coordinated components inside one process.
avoid_when: Only two or three objects interact, or the links are stable: a direct reference or a single callback is simpler than a hub.
A facade or an observer already solves it - facade for one-way access to a subsystem, observer/publisher-subscriber when the need is pure fan-out rather than coordination.
The participants are separate processes or services: use a message broker, a point-to-point or publish-subscribe channel; an in-process mediator does not span a network boundary.
The real problem is a long-running workflow across bounded contexts: a process manager or saga owns that, not an in-memory object hub.
The hub is already accumulating every rule and every piece of state: split it by concern or push behaviour back into the colleagues before adding more.
High-frequency, latency-sensitive interactions (thousands per second): the mediator indirection adds measurable overhead per dispatch.
Simple fire-and-forget pub/sub where no central coordination logic exists: an Event Aggregator or message bus is lighter weight.
anti_patterns: God-object mediator: the hub accumulates every rule and every piece of state until it is the program and the colleagues only carry data.
Bypass: colleagues that call each other directly 'just this once', silently restoring the many-to-many web the pattern removed.
Reaching through the hub: the mediator manipulating colleague internals (fields, private methods) instead of their public interface, which recreates the coupling on a different level.
Global or singleton mediator used as a service locator, coupling every colleague to one static instance and destroying the reuse the pattern was applied for.
A mediator per colleague pair that merely forwards A to B, keeping the same number of links with extra indirection.

Cyclic mediator dependencies: the mediator depends on a colleague to make routing decisions, but that colleague depends on the mediator for its own coordination — a deadlock-prone circular dependency that is hard to unit-test.

Event storm: the mediator fires one event that triggers handlers which fire more events, creating undocumented chains that are impossible to reason about; Fowler's guidance is to prefer a single line of events or an Event Aggregator over nested event chains.

Synchronous dispatch bottleneck: a synchronous mediator on a single thread serialises all handler execution, so a slow handler (I/O, retries, validation) blocks every other colleague; prefer asynchronous dispatch for I/O-bound participants.

Typed event proliferation: each new interaction adds a new event type to the mediator's interface, growing the public surface until it is as tightly coupled as the original direct-calling code; group events into topics or channels to contain the surface.

Mediator as universal message bus: routing every cross-cutting concern through a single application-wide mediator turns it into a god object; split by bounded context or use a purpose-built event bus instead.
Missing failure semantics: no defined retry policy, timeout, or compensation when a colleague fails to respond; undefined behaviour at the coordination layer.
One mediator per whole application: a single hub handling order processing, user auth, and notification routing simultaneously is a god object by another name; split by domain or bounded context.
design_principles: Program to an interface: colleagues depend on the abstract mediator, never on a concrete hub or on each other.
Single responsibility: the mediator owns interaction, colleagues own their domain behaviour.
Open/closed: new colleagues and new mediation strategies are added without modifying existing participants.
Least knowledge (Law of Demeter): a colleague talks only to its mediator and never to its peers' internals.
Dependency inversion: both colleagues and the concrete hub depend on the mediator abstraction.
Separation of concerns: communication policy is separated from application logic.
Mediator owns interaction policy; colleagues own domain behaviour — keep these concerns strictly separated.
Start coarse-grained: mediate at the level of user intent or business transaction, not at the level of individual field changes; Fowler recommends measuring before adding fine-grained event handling.

Event chains are a code smell — a handler firing another event while processing the first creates invisible control flow that neither the mediator interface nor the colleague interface documents; resolve through explicit mediator methods instead.
Typed over stringly-typed: prefer sealed hierarchies, discriminated unions, or record types for events so refactors are compiler-verified and typos surface as type errors.
Mediator scope should map to a bounded context or workflow, not the whole application; multiple focused mediators beat one god mediator.
Failure semantics must be explicit: retry policy, timeout budget, and compensation behaviour are part of the mediator's contract, not afterthoughts.
Instrument the mediator: since call stacks become harder to follow through indirection, structured logging of sender, event type, handler outcome, and duration is essential for production debugging.
best_practices: Give the mediator one narrow, typed notification entry point (a notify(sender, event) method or a closed event type) and keep it stable.
Colleagues hold the abstract mediator only; never let a colleague know a concrete colleague type, and never let the mediator bypass a colleague's public interface.
Keep domain behaviour in the colleagues - when the mediator starts implementing business rules, push them back or split the hub by concern before it becomes a god object.
Split a growing mediator along event groups or responsibility (dialog coordinator, session router) rather than letting one class coordinate everything.
Make registration explicit and symmetric: every subscribe has an unsubscribe, and teardown paths deregister colleagues.
Hold colleagues weakly or own their lifetime deliberately, and document who owns whom so listeners cannot leak or fire after destruction.
Test colleagues against a stub mediator and the mediator against fake colleagues; the hub is the natural seam for interaction tests.
Define re-entrancy and ordering: state whether dispatch is synchronous, whether a handler may emit, and iterate over a snapshot when handlers can unsubscribe.

Prefer typed, closed event vocabularies (Pydantic models, Scala case classes, TypeScript discriminated unions, C# record types, Java sealed interfaces) over stringly-typed event names so that refactors are compiler-verified and typos surface as type errors rather than silent mis-dispatches.

Make the mediator asynchronous by default when the coordinated participants are I/O-bound or the dispatch graph may branch: async notify/dispatch avoids serialising all handlers on the calling thread and prevents a single slow handler from back-pressuring every colleague.

In CQRS/ES systems, treat the mediator as the command/query router (MediatR style) that dispatches to typed handlers and layers pipeline behaviours for validation, authorisation and logging — keep the routing logic thin and the handler logic rich.

Split a growing mediator along event or use-case groups (dialog coordinator, session router, workflow stage) rather than adding more rules to one class; each sub-mediator becomes a natural test seam and can be replaced independently.

Log or instrument every dispatch path at debug level: mediator indirection makes call stacks harder to follow, so structured logging of sender, event type and handler outcome is essential for production debugging.

Prefer composition over inheritance for the mediator: a mediator built from small, composable notification handlers or a pipeline of behaviours is easier to test and extend than a single class with a large switch/case or if/else chain.

When the coordination rules become a state machine (states, transitions, guards), consider a formal statechart or workflow engine (Camunda, Temporal, Netflix Conductor) rather than encoding complex state in a plain mediator object.
Use explicit intent methods over generic notify: requestLanding, approveTakeoff, pauseWorkflow read better in logs and tests than generic event strings.
Define failure semantics upfront: retry policy, timeout budget, and compensation behaviour must be part of the mediator's documented contract, not afterthoughts added during incident response.

In Java, model interactions as records implementing a sealed interface; use pattern-matching switch for exhaustive, compiler-verified dispatch. In TypeScript, use discriminated unions. In C#, use record types and a switch expression.

Guard against circular re-entrancy: a component A notifying the mediator triggering an update to component B whose change handler also notifies the mediator can loop indefinitely; use a re-entrancy guard flag.
For cross-team or cross-bounded-context workflows, prefer a durable workflow engine (Temporal, Camunda) over a hand-rolled in-memory mediator, because process state must survive process restarts.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) - Mediator, Behavioral Patterns chapter (intent, participants, consequences: decoupled colleagues, centralised control, mediator complexity).

Martin Fowler, 'Event Aggregator', Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2004): https://martinfowler.com/eaaDev/EventAggregator.html — Event Aggregator channels events from multiple objects through a single hub, simplifying client registration; Fowler notes it is a particular form of Facade focused on observer relationships, and cautions about observer's memory-management dangers.

Martin Fowler, 'Mediated Synchronization', Enterprise Application Architecture (2004): https://martinfowler.com/eaaDev/MediatedSynchronization.html — Multiple screens observe a shared domain data store; Fowler recommends starting coarse-grained and warns against event chains within a layer, advocating observer relationships only across layers (presentation observes domain).

Derick Bailey, 'Event Aggregator And/Or/vs Mediator: A Tale of Two Patterns', Los Techies (2013): https://lostechies.com/derickbailey/2013/03/18/event-aggregator-andorvs-mediator-a-tale-of-two-patterns/ — Key distinction: Event Aggregator forwards events with no central workflow logic; Mediator encapsulates complex coordination, business rules and process logic that decides when and how to call other objects. Often both patterns are combined in one system.

Muhammad Rizwan, 'CQRS and MediatR in .NET: When It Is Worth It and When It Is Not' (2025): https://rizwancode.com/blog/cqrs-mediatr-in-dotnet — In-process mediator (MediatR) pairs naturally with CQRS; pipeline behaviors centralize cross-cutting concerns (validation, logging, caching); use commands for writes, queries for reads; avoid when simple CRUD suffices.

C# Corner, 'Real-World MediatR Patterns and Common Mistakes in ASP.NET Core' (2025): https://www.c-sharpcorner.com/article/real-world-mediatr-patterns-and-common-mistakes-in-asp-net-core — MediatR decouples controllers from business logic; keep handlers single-purpose and grouped by feature; inject only necessary dependencies; use pipeline behaviors for shared concerns rather than wrapping repository methods.

Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Messaging, Message Router, Pipes and Filters, Process Manager (2003): https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/ — The routing patterns catalog shows how Mediator and Message Router pattern families solve increasingly complex routing needs; Process Manager extends Mediator with durable state for multi-step workflows; Messaging Mapper separates domain objects from message format.

Nelson Alfonso, 'Implementing the Mediator Pattern in TypeScript: A Comprehensive Guide', Medium (2024): https://medium.com/@Nelsonalfonso/implementing-the-mediatr-pattern-in-typescript-a-comprehensive-guide-3c20fdc27af0 — TypeScript implementation of MediatR-style mediator with DI, typed requests/handlers, and React/Angular backend/frontend examples.

Jitin Kayyala, 'Mediator Design Pattern in Java: Implementation, Examples & Best Practices 2026', Javarevisited/Medium (2026): https://medium.com/javarevisited/revisiting-the-mediator-pattern-in-java-25-structuring-complex-component-interactions-fc743c1d9d03 — Java 17+ sealed interfaces with pattern-matching switch dispatch for exhaustive, type-safe event hierarchies.

Krzysztof Woyke, 'The Mediator Design Pattern in Java', Baeldung (2019): https://www.baeldung.com/java-mediator-pattern — Classic GoF Mediator implementation in Java with Button/Fan/PowerSupplier example; covers SRP and OCP benefits.

Francisco Andres Almarza Menjiba et al., 'Software component development based on the mediator pattern design: the interactive graphic organizer case', IEEE (2011): https://doi.org/10.1109/tla.2011.6129710 — Empirical case study showing mediator pattern reduced coupling in a NASA LaSRS++ flight simulation framework, improving component reuse.

Amel Bennaceur & Valérie Issarny, 'Automated Synthesis of Mediators to Support Component Interoperability', IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering (2014): https://doi.org/10.1109/tse.2014.2364844 — Formal approach to automated mediator synthesis using ontology reasoning and constraint programming to infer interface mappings and coordinate behaviours automatically.

Garces et al., 'Software Mediators as First-class Entities of Systems-of-Systems Software Architectures', Springer (2019): https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1186/s13173-019-0089-3.pdf — MediArch three-layered mediator architecture (communication, conversion, control) for Systems-of-Systems; demonstrates mediators as first-class architectural entities enabling continuous integration and evolution.

Kevin Cunningham, 'Use of the Mediator Design Pattern in the LaSRS++ framework', NASA (1999): https://doi.org/10.2514/6.1999-4336 — NASA LaSRS++ flight simulation case study; mediator as information broker between simulation software components achieving reusability, simplicity and testability.

Hridesh Rajan, 'One More Step in the Direction of Modularized Integration Concerns', ICSE (2004): https://lab-design.github.io/papers/ICSE-2004/modularize-integration.pdf — Mediator-based design for behavioural relationship modularisation; maps mediator approach to AspectJ and identifies need for instance-level aspects as mediators.
DevIQ, 'Domain Events Pattern', DevIQ: https://deviq.com/ — Domain Events pattern and its relationship to Mediator for coordinating cross-aggregate state changes in DDD applications.

Pavan Rangani, 'Saga Pattern in Microservices: Orchestration vs Choreography Complete Guide' (2026): https://pavanrangani.com/blog/saga-pattern-microservices-orchestration-choreography — Comprehensive guide comparing saga orchestration (mediator) vs choreography for distributed transactions; covers outbox pattern, idempotency, compensation design, and when to use workflow engines.

Matthew Palma, 'Distributed sagas: choreography vs orchestration in production systems' (2026): https://matthewpalma.dev/blog/distributed-sagas-choreography-vs-orchestration — Production failure modes of both approaches; emphasises that orchestration is a mediator variant with durability and compensation requirements; choreography distributes decision-making at the cost of implicit state.

NILUS, 'Saga Orchestration vs Choreography in Distributed Systems' (2025): https://www.nilus.be/blog/saga_orchestration_vs_choreography_in_distributed_systems/ — Practical guidance on using orchestration for mission-critical workflows with explicit milestones and choreography for independent domain reactions; emphasises that Kafka solves transport, not process semantics.

Gang of Four Mediator pattern reference (UNC mirror): https://www.cs.unc.edu/~stotts/GOF/hires/pat5e.htm — canonical intent, applicability, participants and consequences, including the trade-off that centralized control can make the mediator complex.

MediatR official repository: https://github.com/LuckyPennySoftware/MediatR?tab=readme-ov-file — documents a simple .NET in-process mediator with typed requests/responses, commands, queries, notifications, events and handler registration.

MassTransit Mediator official documentation: https://masstransit-v7.netlify.app/usage/mediator.html — documents transport-free in-process/in-memory mediation, Send versus Publish semantics, request timeouts, runtime consumer connection and middleware.

Software Engineering Stack Exchange, 'How to prevent a Mediator from becoming a God Object': https://softwareengineering.stackexchange.com/questions/369690/how-to-prevent-a-mediator-from-becoming-a-god-object — criticism and remedy for over-broad mediators: split responsibilities around the Single Responsibility Principle.

related_patterns_notes.observer: Mediator and Observer are often combined: colleagues use observer subscriptions to notify the mediator. However, Observer is one-to-many fan-out with no central coordination logic, while Mediator encapsulates complex decision-making about which colleagues react and in what order. Mediator knows the workflow; a Subject in Observer does not; distinction: Observer is one-to-many broadcast; Mediator is many-to-many routing through a central coordinator that decides consequences.
related_patterns_notes.facade: Both introduce an intermediary. Facade provides a simplified unidirectional interface to a subsystem (clients call facade, facade calls subsystem internals). Mediator enables cooperative behaviour between colleagues that could not or would not provide it themselves, with multidirectional communication; distinction: Facade is one-way access (client → facade → subsystem); Mediator is multi-directional coordination among peers.
related_patterns_notes.event-aggregator: Event Aggregator (Fowler) channels events from multiple objects through a single hub so clients register with one object instead of many. It is a particular form of Facade focused on observer relationships. Unlike Mediator, an Event Aggregator contains no workflow logic — it only forwards events without deciding who reacts or in what order; distinction: Event Aggregator forwards blindly; Mediator encapsulates coordination logic and decides consequences.
related_patterns_notes.command: Commands and Mediator often combine: a command is a typed request that the mediator routes to a handler. MediatR exemplifies this pairing. Commands are the request side of CQRS; the mediator handles the routing decision; distinction: Command encapsulates an action as an object; Mediator decides which command handler to invoke.
related_patterns_notes.chain-of-responsibility: Both pass a request along a chain of handlers. Chain of Responsibility lets multiple objects handle a request without the sender knowing which one does; the chain itself decides termination. Mediator centralises the decision in one object that knows all colleagues and their ordering; distinction: Chain of Responsibility is decentralised (any handler may handle); Mediator centralises the routing decision.
related_patterns_notes.publisher-subscriber: Pub/Sub and Mediator both use an intermediary to decouple senders from receivers. Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget with unknown subscribers; the publisher does not know who (if anyone) handles its message. Mediator is aware of its colleagues and orchestrates their reactions; distinction: Pub/Sub has no guaranteed handler and no orchestration; Mediator coordinates specific colleague reactions.
related_patterns_notes.message-router: Message Router (Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns) is the distributed equivalent of Mediator — it decides message destinations based on content without modifying the message. Process Manager extends this with stateful, multi-step coordination across services; distinction: Message Router routes based on content; Process Manager holds state and drives multi-step workflows across service boundaries.
related_patterns_notes.process-manager: Saga uses an orchestrator (a mediator variant) to drive distributed transactions across services with compensating transactions for rollback. The orchestrator is the concrete mediator in the saga. Unlike an in-memory mediator, saga orchestrators are typically durable and recoverable; distinction: Saga orchestrator is a mediator specialised for long-running distributed transactions with explicit compensation and durability requirements. Process Manager (EIP) is a stateful mediator that routes messages through a sequence of steps, deciding the next step based on message content and internal state. It is the enterprise-scale realisation of the Mediator pattern for cross-service workflows; distinction: Process Manager is a Mediator scaled to distributed, long-running, multi-step workflows across service boundaries.
